summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in France proper.

No provision of that framework restricts a trans or same-sex visitor. Same-sex marriage has been available since 2013, legal gender-marker change requires neither surgery nor sterilisation, gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery have been available under French law since 1975, the statute covering discrimination on grounds of gender identity is in force, and the French ban on conversion practices adopted in 2023 applies.

Two limits sit alongside that coverage. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary status has no legal counterpart on arrival. Gender-affirming care is delivered in a jurisdiction of about 8 square miles and roughly 10,000 residents, and the single red flag recorded against Saint Barthélemy in an aggregate travel-safety rating is limited healthcare access; prescriptions and ongoing treatment cannot be assumed to be available locally.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. French prison administration policy recognises only biological sex for placement, and trans detainees, overwhelmingly women, are held under birth sex; a 2011 case in Nantes placed a trans woman in a men's prison. The controller-general of detention places, in an opinion of 25 May 2021 drawing on about 40 referrals received since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention.

Socially the territory is discreet rather than permissive: it has no LGBTQ venues, no Pride events and no visible scene, same-sex couples attract no attention, crime is low and no hostility toward gay or trans visitors is noted in the sources.
tangentialFactors:
An aggregate travel-safety rating for Saint Barthélemy stands at 7.7 out of 10, counting nine positive rights against one red flag: legal gender change without surgery and anti-discrimination law are in place, healthcare access is not.

No government LGBT+ travel advice covers Saint Barthélemy, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office lists no warnings for the territory; no trans-specific visitor tips have been submitted either. The absence of an official warning reflects the absence of an assessment.

The detention findings come from reporting and oversight applied to the French prison system as a whole, so they describe the conditions a trans person would face in the metropole as well as under the same administration elsewhere.

The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples. Guests are high-end and discreet, staff at major properties are trained for diverse guests, and the lack of any organised scene means visibility is low rather than contested.
